title: Facial Massage at Home: A 5-Minute Routine and What It Does — cv.cm
description: How to do a facial massage at home: clean hands, light upward strokes, jaw muscle release, a 5-minute routine, what studies show, and when to skip it for skin.
h1: How do you do a facial massage at home?
answer: Wash your hands and face, warm a few drops of oil or cream between your fingers, then use light, slow strokes that move up and out: forehead to temples, along the brows, across the cheeks, and along the jaw. Add gentle circles on the jaw muscle if you clench. Five minutes is enough. Facial massage may help you relax, but it does not remove wrinkles.

ol: Remove makeup and wash your face with a mild cleanser. Wash your hands too, and keep your nails short so they do not scratch.
Choose a slip product: a few drops of a plain facial oil, a moisturizer or a cream you already use without problems. You need just enough for the fingers to glide without pulling the skin.
Warm the product between your fingertips for a few seconds.
Sit in front of a mirror or lie down with your head on a pillow. Relax your shoulders and let your jaw hang slightly open, teeth apart.

body: Pressure on the face is lighter than anywhere else on the body. On a 1 to 10 scale, aim for 2 to 3 on the skin of the cheeks and around the eyes, and 4 to 5 on the jaw muscle. Light pressure moves only the skin. Medium pressure moves the muscle under it. You should never feel the skin being dragged.
Most routines use the same direction: from the center of the face outward, and from lower to higher. This direction is a comfortable convention, not a way to move fat or lift the face.

head: Area
What to do
Pressure
rows: Place the flat fingers of both hands at the center of the forehead. Glide outward to the temples, then move up a little and repeat until you reach the hairline.
Pinch along each eyebrow gently with thumb and index finger, from the inner end to the outer end. Stay on the brow bone.
With the ring finger, tap very lightly along the bony rim under the eye, from the inner corner outward. Never press on the eyeball.
Place the fingertips beside the nose and glide outward under the cheekbone toward the ears.
Make slow circles on the soft area beside the outer end of each brow.
Glide the knuckles or fingers from the chin along the lower edge of the jaw to just below the ears.
Clench your teeth briefly to feel the muscle bulge between the cheekbone and the angle of the jaw. Relax the jaw, then make small circles on the muscle.

body.note: Do not press or stroke the front of the neck. If you include the neck, use only very light downward strokes on the sides, below the ears, and keep away from the windpipe and the pulse.

body: Many people clench their teeth when they concentrate or feel stressed. The masseter, the strong chewing muscle at the back of the cheek, can then feel tight or sore. The NHS lists massaging the painful jaw muscles among the self-care steps for jaw joint problems (temporomandibular disorder), along with soft food, a warm or cold pack and relaxation.

Two acupressure points sit on or near this muscle. Locations follow the WHO Standard Acupuncture Point Locations in the Western Pacific Region (2008). In traditional Chinese medicine they are linked to the jaw. Here they are simply useful landmarks for the muscle.

body: If you grind your teeth at night, have sensitive or worn teeth, or have pain in the jaw, face or ear, see a dentist. Massage may ease muscle tightness for a while, but it does not stop grinding or protect the teeth.
Do this in the evening after cleansing, or any time you notice tension in your face. If you want to keep to the times, use a timer, for example cv.cm's countdown.

body: Research on facial massage is small. A 2022 pilot study in Japan used CT scans on five healthy adults who massaged their faces twice a day for two weeks and reported small changes in cheek tissue shape. With only five people, no control group and a short follow-up, it cannot show a lasting effect. A 2024 pilot study of 62 women with sleep complaints, who did a daily cosmetic facial self-massage for two months, reported better sleep and well-being scores. It was also small and is best read as a sign that the routine was relaxing.

Many people notice that the face looks less puffy and a little pinker right after a massage. This is short-lived. There is no good evidence that facial massage removes wrinkles, permanently lifts or slims the face, or changes the shape of the jaw. Treat it as a calming routine and a way to apply skin care, not as an anti-aging treatment.

sections.h: Skin precautions and when to skip it

ul: Active acne or breakouts: skip the affected area. Rubbing inflamed spots can spread irritation and leave marks.
Rosacea or easily flushed skin: use only very light pressure, few strokes and no heat, or skip it if your face reddens.
Eczema, a rash, sunburn, cold sores, cuts or any infected skin: do not massage that area until it has healed.
After cosmetic procedures such as fillers, botulinum toxin injections, peels or laser: ask the clinic how long to wait before massaging the face.
Blood thinners or easy bruising: very light pressure only.
New oil or cream: test a small amount on the jaw line for a day before using it on the whole face.

body: Hard tools and vigorous pressure can cause harm. A 2024 case report described a ruptured neck muscle (platysma) in a woman who had used a hard wooden block for facial massage over a long period. Gentle hands are enough.

body.note: Stop and see a doctor if you notice sudden weakness or drooping of one side of the face, numbness, or trouble speaking: this is an emergency. See a doctor or dentist if jaw pain lasts more than a few weeks, if your jaw locks or you cannot open your mouth fully, or if you have facial swelling with fever.

ul: Dragging dry skin: add a few more drops of oil or cream so the fingers glide.
Pressing hard on the cheeks to "lift" them: pressure does not lift tissue. Use light glides instead.
Pressing near the eye: stay on the bone rim and use the ring finger, the weakest finger.
Long sessions with many products: five minutes with one product is plenty. If your skin feels sore or red the next day, halve the time and pressure.
Clenching during the massage: keep the teeth slightly apart and the tongue resting behind the lower teeth.

faq.q: Does facial massage get rid of wrinkles?
faq.a: No good study shows that facial massage removes wrinkles or permanently tightens skin. It may make the face look fresher for a short time and many people find it relaxing.

faq.q: Should you massage your face up or down?
faq.a: Most routines use outward and upward strokes for comfort and consistency. The direction does not lift the face, so choose what feels gentle and do not drag the skin.

faq.q: How often should you do a facial massage?
faq.a: A few minutes once a day is common. If your skin becomes red, irritated or breaks out, cut back or stop.

faq.q: Can facial massage slim the face or the jaw?
faq.a: No. Massage does not remove fat or shrink muscle. Easing a tight jaw muscle may make the jaw feel more relaxed, but the shape stays the same.

faq.q: Is it better to use oil or cream for facial massage?
faq.a: Either is fine if your skin tolerates it. Use a small amount of a product you already use, and choose a lighter, non-comedogenic product if you get breakouts.
